sections.heading: European trade establishments on the Andhra coast

blocks.text: Andhra's 974-km coast, with **Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam)** as the Golconda kingdom's great port ('Maisolos' to the Greeks — the coast's textile-diamond outlet), drew every European company. The prize: **kalamkari/chintz textiles, indigo, diamonds (Golconda's Kollur mines), saltpetre** — Coromandel cloth was the currency that bought Southeast Asian spices.

rows: **Dutch (VOC)**
**Masulipatnam (1605)** — their first Coromandel factory; Nizampatnam (Petapuli), Palakollu, Draksharama, Jaggernaikpuram (Kakinada), **Bimlipatam (Bheemunipatnam, 1652)**
Dominated 17th-century Coromandel trade; Bimlipatam's Dutch cemetery survives — prelims-friendly relic
**English (EIC)**
**Masulipatnam (1611)** — the Company's **first Coromandel factory** (before Madras, 1639); **Armagon/Durgarazpatnam (1626)**; later Visakhapatnam (1682-)
The 'golden firman' of Golconda (1632/34) eased trade; Masulipatnam's 1686-87 Mughal-conquest disruptions pushed primacy to Madras
**French**
**Masulipatnam & Yanam (1723/1731)**
**Yanam remained French till 1954** — the Andhra dot of French India; Bussy's 1750s hinterland presence (Circars grant to the French, 1753) the high-water mark
Danes/others
Minor Coromandel touchpoints
Peripheral to Andhra

blocks.text: **The power transition**: Anglo-French Carnatic Wars decided the coast — after **Bussy's** Hyderabad ascendancy, **Forde's capture of Masulipatnam (1759)** during the Third Carnatic War evicted French influence; the **Nizam granted the Northern Circars to the English (firman 1766; treaty 1768)**, and Rayalaseema followed as the **Ceded Districts (1800)** — trade posts had become territorial rule.

sections.heading: Andhra under Company rule — the colonial re-ordering

items: **Administrative grid**: Circars + Ceded Districts organised into Madras Presidency collectorates; **Munro's ryotwari** (from the Ceded Districts' laboratory) alongside the **permanent-settlement zamindaris** of the coast (Vizianagaram, Pithapuram, Nuzvid, Venkatagiri sanads, 1802-03) — the dual tenure world (HCOI-028's AP paragraph).

**Early resistance**: **palegar (poligar) suppressions** in the Ceded Districts (Munro's disarmament); zamindari revolts — the **Vizianagaram raja's stand at Padmanabham (1794)**; **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's rising (1846-47)**; the agency's first fituris — the resistance thread predating 1857.

**Economic re-ordering**: handloom decline under Manchester imports (Masulipatnam's long fade — sealed by the catastrophic **1864 cyclone**, ~30,000+ deaths); **Godavari-Krishna anicuts (Cotton, 1852; Prakasam barrage's ancestor 1855)** creating the delta's canal economy and grain-export surplus; groundnut-indigo-tobacco commercialisation; railways (Madras line through the south; coastal line by 1890s) reorienting trade to Madras — Andhra as agrarian hinterland of a Presidency capital it would later demand separation from.
**The answer frame**: ports → factories → wars → firmans → settlements → resistance → re-ordering: one continuous arc from 1605 Masulipatnam to the Madras Presidency's Andhra districts.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Frame Company-era Andhra as a hinterland being made — port to presidency, weaver to ryot, palegar to pensioner — transformation, not mere chronology, is what the mains examiner grades.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — European trade & Company Andhra

items: **Trade footholds:** the **Dutch (Pulicat, Nizampatnam), the English (Masulipatnam 1611 — their first factory on the Coromandel/east coast, then Madras 1639), and the French (Yanam)** — the Andhra coast was central to the Coromandel textile trade (famous painted cloth, *kalamkari*).

**Into rule:** after Buxar and the Northern Circars grant (**the Circars ceded 1765-66**), coastal Andhra passed to the Company; **Rayalaseema (the Ceded Districts) came in 1800** from the Nizam ('Datta Mandalam').

**Colonial economy:** ryotwari revenue (Munro), decline of handloom weaving under de-industrialisation, and later the transformative **Godavari & Krishna anicuts (Sir Arthur Cotton)** turning the deltas into a rice bowl.
**Significance:** Andhra's colonial experience combined coastal commercial prominence with agrarian transformation and artisanal decline.

**Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema)** transferred by the Nizam to the Company in **1800**; the Northern Circars earlier.
**Sir Arthur Cotton** — Dowleswaram anicut on the Godavari.

**Dutch at Masulipatnam 1605; Bheemunipatnam (Bimlipatam) 1652** — Dutch relics survive there.
**Yanam** — French from 1723/31, transferred de facto **1954** (de jure 1962); now in Puducherry UT.
**Forde captured Masulipatnam (1759)**; **Northern Circars to EIC — firman 1766, confirmed 1768**; **Ceded Districts 1800**.
**Battle of Padmanabham (1794)** — Vizianagaram's Chinna Vijayaramaraju fell resisting the Company.
**Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's rising 1846-47** (Koilkuntla-Kurnool belt); executed 1847.
**Dowleswaram anicut (Godavari) 1852; Krishna anicut 1855** — Sir Arthur Cotton; the **1864 Masulipatnam cyclone** (~30,000+ dead).
Golconda's **Kollur mines** yielded the Koh-i-noor-class diamonds that made Masulipatnam famous.
mainsAngles: Masulipatnam was the Coromandel's gateway — trace the European contest for the Andhra coast from 1605 to 1766.
From firman to collectorate — how did trade concessions become territorial rule over the Circars and Rayalaseema?

Explain how colonial administrative geography (Presidency, tenures, railways) set up the later demand for a separate Andhra.

glossary.definition: The textile-centred commerce of India's southeast coast — Andhra's kalamkari and chintz the currency of Indo-Southeast Asian exchange.
A fortified warehouse-residence of a European company — Masulipatnam hosting Dutch (1605) and English (1611) firsts on the Coromandel.
A royal grant/charter (Golconda's 'golden firman', the Mughal-Nizam grants) licensing trade or ceding revenue rights.
Armed local chieftain of the southern uplands; the Ceded Districts' palegar suppression was Munro's first campaign.
The five coastal Andhra sarkars (Chicacole to Guntur) obtained from the Nizam (1766) — the Presidency's Andhra spine.
The scheduled hill areas of the Eastern Ghats under special regulations — the fituris' home and today's Fifth Schedule areas.

blocks.text: Christian missions reached Andhra early (Jesuit touches) but institutionalised after 1813's Charter opening: **London Missionary Society (Visakhapatnam, 1805)**, **CMS (Machilipatnam, 1841)**, American Baptists (Nellore-Ongole — the 'Lone Star' mission; **Ongole's mass conversions among Madigas, 1870s** under J.E. Clough, tank-work famine relief 1876-78), Lutherans (Guntur, 1842 — **C.F. Heyer**), Canadian Baptists (north coast). By-products that outlived evangelism: **schools & colleges** (**Noble College, Machilipatnam 1843**; St. Aloysius Vizag; Guntur's AELC institutions), **girls' education pioneering**, printing presses & Telugu grammars-dictionaries, medical missions, and the **Dalit uplift channel** — conversion as an exit from untouchability (the Ongole movement's social meaning), which pressured caste-Hindu reform in response.

rows: **Social reform**
**Veeresalingam's Rajahmundry hub** (full note HCOA-059); Brahmo networks (Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu's purity-social work); Vivekananda's 1893-97 ripples
Widow remarriage (1881), anti-nautch, anti-dowry, girls' schools — reform's Telugu edition
**Literary renaissance**
**Kandukuri (prose's workhorse), Gurajada (Kanyasulkam 1892; 'Desamunu Preminchumanna'), Gidugu (vyavaharika movement)**, Chilakamarthi (Gayopakhyanam), Rayaprolu & the bhava kavitvam wave
From pandit-Telugu to people's Telugu; literature as reform's vehicle — the play, the novel, the essay all debut socially armed
**Press & associations**
Vivekavardhini (1874), Krishna Patrika (1902), Andhra Patrika (1908/14); libraries & night schools; caste-reform sabhas and **adi-movements** (Adi-Andhra 1917)
The infrastructure of a Telugu public sphere (HCOA-060 completes)

sections.heading: Reading the awakening — dynamics and debates

items: **The triangle**: missionary challenge → colonial education's new class → indigenous reform response — Andhra's renaissance was reactive AND creative: it borrowed the school, the press and the association, and filled them with Telugu content.

**Social depth question**: reform began Brahmin-led (Kandukuri's circle) but was **widened from below** — missionary-Dalit movements, Adi-Andhra assertion (Bhagya Reddy Varma's Hyderabad lineage; coastal Adi-Andhra conferences from **1917 (Vijayawada)** renaming Panchamas as Adi-Andhras in the 1921 census), and non-Brahmin currents (Justice Party's Andhra wing) — a multi-front awakening, not a single stream.

**Language as the battleground**: Gidugu's spoken-Telugu campaign democratised print exactly when mass politics needed a mass language — the awakening's most consequential technical victory (school textbooks, newspapers shifting to vyavaharika).

**Assessment**: by 1920 Andhra possessed the full modern kit — colleges, presses, associations, reformed language, reform causes — which is why Gandhi's movements found here their readiest province; the awakening was nationalism's dress rehearsal.

Always argue the triangle (challenge-class-response) and the from-below widening — the two analytical moves that lift this beyond a names list.

blocks.text: Exam tip: 'The missionaries brought the tools; Andhra forged its own awakening with them' — that thesis line, the Ongole-Dalit paragraph, and Gidugu's language victory are this note's three scoring pillars.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — missionaries & the Andhra awakening

items: **Missionary contribution:** printing presses, schools, Telugu grammar & dictionaries, and mass education among the poor and Dalits — an ambivalent legacy of modernisation alongside evangelism.

**The Andhra renaissance:** **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** ('the father of the Telugu renaissance') — widow remarriage, women's education, anti-nautch, and modern Telugu prose (*Rajasekhara Charitramu*, the first Telugu novel).
**Debates:** reform from within vs Westernised modernity; social reform's urban-elite reach vs mass impact.
**Significance:** the awakening created the cultural-intellectual base for Andhra's later linguistic and political self-assertion.

prelimsPointers: **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** — pioneer of widow remarriage and women's education in Andhra; wrote *Rajasekhara Charitramu*.
Missionaries pioneered **Telugu printing, grammar and mass schooling**.
**London Missionary Society at Visakhapatnam: 1805** — Andhra's first Protestant station.
**Noble College, Machilipatnam (CMS): 1843** — Robert Turlington Noble; among coastal Andhra's earliest colleges.
**C.F. Heyer** (first American Lutheran missionary) — **Guntur mission, 1842**.
**Ongole Baptist ('Lone Star') mission — J.E. Clough**; mass Madiga conversions during the **1876-78 famine** (Buckingham Canal work relief).
**Adi-Andhra movement**: first conference **Vijayawada 1917**; 'Adi-Andhra' entered the **1921 census** nomenclature.
**Kanyasulkam (Gurajada, 1892)** — dedicated against bride-price; first great modern Telugu play.
**Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy** — spoken-Telugu (vyavaharika) crusade; his birthday (29 Aug) is **Telugu Language Day**.
**Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu** — Brahmo 'social purity' movement, anti-nautch; Pithapuram Rajah's college principal.
mainsAngles: Missionary enterprise in Andhra converted fewer souls than it educated — assess its by-products for the region's awakening.
The Andhra renaissance was reaction and creation at once — analyse the triangle of challenge, class and response.
Dalit conversion movements were social protest by other means — examine the Ongole phenomenon and Adi-Andhra assertion.
Language reform was social reform's infrastructure — evaluate Gidugu's spoken-Telugu victory.
Why was Andhra nationalism's readiest province by 1920? Argue from the awakening's completed toolkit.

The self-chosen census identity (from 1917-21) of Andhra Dalits claiming original-inhabitant status — assertion through nomenclature.
Campaign against dedicating girls (devadasi) and nautch entertainments — Venkataratnam Naidu's signature cause.
Spoken-standard Telugu championed by Gidugu for print and schooling against archaic granthika.
The lyric-romantic movement of modern Telugu poetry (Rayaprolu et al.) — the renaissance's aesthetic wing.
Brahmo-inflected reform (Venkataratnam Naidu) targeting drink, nautch and vice — respectability as reform idiom.

sections.heading: Three Company servants who shaped Andhra's memory

rows: **Sir Thomas Munro (1761-1827)**

Read's assistant (Baramahal) → **Principal Collector, Ceded Districts (1800-07)** — palegar pacification, village-level ryotwari settlements → **Governor of Madras (1820-27)**; died of cholera at **Pattikonda (Kurnool), 6 July 1827**

**Ryotwari's architect** — direct patta to the cultivator; judicial-revenue integration (collector-magistrate); the 'Munro system' of paternalist district officer; folk deification in Rayalaseema (the 'Mandava' legends; equestrian statue, Madras) — the coloniser remembered as protector: a paradox worth one line
**Colin Mackenzie (1754-1821)**
Military engineer-surveyor; **Mysore & Deccan surveys**; **first Surveyor-General of India (1815)**

The **Mackenzie Manuscripts**: with Brahmin assistants (**Kavali brothers — Venkata Boriah, Lakshmayya**) collected **thousands of local histories, kaifiyats (village records), inscriptions, coins** across Telugu country — the single richest archive of Andhra's pre-colonial past; 'surveyed the land and salvaged its memory'
Company civilian at **Cuddapah/Kadapa**; judge-collector posts; spent private fortune on Telugu letters

**Telugu-English (1852) & English-Telugu dictionaries**; **rescued and edited Vemana's verses** (first print 1829); collected-copied thousands of Telugu manuscripts (his 'Brown's pandits' scriptorium at Kadapa); grammar, translations — called **'the saviour of Telugu literature'** at its lowest ebb; the **C.P. Brown Library, Kadapa** preserves the memory

sections.heading: Reading them together — administration, archive, language

items: **Three faces of colonial knowledge**: Munro = **governing knowledge** (settlement records, village accounts as the state's eyes); Mackenzie = **historical knowledge** (the survey-archive impulse); Brown = **philological knowledge** (dictionary-edition-grammar) — together the 'colonial knowledge project' that both served empire AND became the raw material of Telugu self-discovery: the renaissance quoted Brown's Vemana and Mackenzie's kaifiyats back at the coloniser.

**The critical balance**: paternalism is still rule (Munro's ryotwari over-assessed for decades); the archive selected and framed (Mackenzie's Brahmin mediation shaped what was 'history'); philology standardised (Brown's choices privileged certain registers) — appreciate the gifts, name the power.

**Legacy institutions**: ryotwari's district-collector state (AP's administrative DNA), the Mackenzie collection (Madras Oriental Manuscripts Library → Chennai's GOML, a research base for Andhra history), Brown's dictionaries (still the reference lineage) and the Kadapa library-revival (1987 onward) — living monuments all three.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the Company servants who shaped Andhra

items: **Thomas Munro** — architect of the **Ryotwari** system in the Ceded Districts/Rayalaseema; the paternalist district administration model.
**Sir Arthur Cotton** — engineer of the **Godavari (Dowleswaram) and Krishna anicuts**, still revered in the deltas as a near-deity for ending famine and creating the rice economy.
**C.P. Brown** — scholar-official who revived Telugu literature (rescuing Vemana's verses, compiling dictionaries) — the colonial servant as custodian of Telugu heritage.
**Reading them together:** administration (Munro), engineering/economy (Cotton), and culture (Brown) — three faces of the colonial encounter that reshaped Andhra.

prelimsPointers: **C.P. Brown** — revived Telugu literature; compiled Telugu-English dictionaries; edited Vemana.
**Thomas Munro** (Ryotwari) and **Arthur Cotton** (anicuts) transformed Andhra's administration and agriculture.
**Munro**: Principal Collector of the **Ceded Districts (1800)**; **Governor of Madras 1820-27**; died at **Pattikonda, Kurnool (1827)**.
**Ryotwari** generalised across Madras during Munro's governorship (1820s) after his Ceded-Districts model.
**Mackenzie**: **first Surveyor-General of India (1815)**; his Telugu-country collection (kaifiyats, inscriptions) assembled with the **Kavali brothers**.
**Kaifiyat** = village historical account/record — the Mackenzie collection's Andhra core.
**C.P. Brown**: served at **Kadapa**; **printed Vemana (1829)**; **Telugu-English dictionary 1852**; 'Browndeepika' tradition; **C.P. Brown Library, Kadapa**.
Brown's pandit-scriptorium copied thousands of Telugu manuscripts at his own expense.
Mackenzie's manuscripts now anchor the **Government Oriental Manuscripts Library (Chennai)** holdings.
mainsAngles: Munro, Mackenzie and Brown embodied three faces of colonial knowledge — governing, archiving, philological: analyse with their Andhra work.
The ryotwari state was Munro's monument — assess his system and the paradox of his folk deification.
Mackenzie's kaifiyats made village memory into archive — evaluate the collection and its Indian co-authors.
C.P. Brown found Telugu letters moribund and left them living — estimate his rescue of Vemana and the language.
Colonial knowledge served the empire and seeded the renaissance — argue with these three careers.

glossary.definition: Village-level historical narrative/record collected in the Mackenzie survey — Andhra's grassroots archive of dynasties, tanks, temples and tenures.
The title-cum-revenue document issued directly to the cultivator — Munro's instrument of the intermediary-free settlement.
Head of India's mapping establishment — Mackenzie the first (1815), uniting cartography with antiquarian collection.
Venkata Boriah and Lakshmayya — Mackenzie's Telugu interpreter-scholars, the Indian intelligence of the archive.
The iconoclast Telugu poet-saint of aphoristic verse (Ataveladi metre) whose corpus Brown collected, edited and first printed.
The dictionary-grammar-edition scholarship (Brown's mode) that standardised and preserved languages — power and gift entwined.
